YHWH’s Covenant: Why Moses Calls Heaven and Earth as Witnesses

Unlike human kings, YHWH does not need witnesses and enforcers. However, Moses in Deuteronomy draws on formulations found in ancient Near Eastern treaties.

Last Updated: September 7, 2026

  1. For a detailed analysis of the treaty texts in their cultural and historical contexts, see Kenneth A. Kitchen and Paul L. N. Lawrence, Treaty, Law and Covenant in the Ancient Near East, 3 vols. (Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 2012).

  2. Moshe Weinfeld was among the first scholars to make these connections. See his Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomic School (Oxford: Clarendon, 1972). Editor’s note: For more on the Deuteronomy and ancient treaty traditions, see Melissa Ramos, “The Making of a Covenant: The Book of Deuteronomy,” TheTorah (2022); Deena Grant, “Loving God Beyond the Way You Love Ashurbanipal,” TheTorah (2016); and Pamela Barmash, “The Novel Introduction of Blessings into our Treaty with God,” TheTorah (2014).

  3. For a collection of the Hittite treaties, see Gary Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts, SBLWAW 7 (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1996).

  4. Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts, 28–29.

  5. KTK is a place name, but its identity is not certain.

  6. See the English edition of the Aramaic text, with references to biblical parallels, in Joseph A. Fitzmyer, trans., “The Inscriptions of Bar-Ga’yah and Mati’el from Sefire,” The Context of Scripture 2.82 (W. Hallo and K. L. Younger, eds. [Leiden: Brill, 2000]), 213–215. Note that the end of the word “Heaven” and the entire word “Earth” are placed in square brackets to indicate that they are modern restorations of parts of the text that are no longer legible. The restoration of the word “Heaven” is extremely secure: the text preserves the letters שמי, the first letters of the Aramaic word for “Heaven” (cognate to Hebrew שמים [shamayim]), so that only the last letter is missing. Based on that, restoration of the word “Earth” is very reasonable, because it forms a natural pair for “Heaven.” The presence of another pair, “day and night,” in the preserved text that follows further supports this. For more details, see the edition of the text itself: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Inscriptions of Sefire (Rome: Pontifical Biblical Insittute, 1995), especially p. 76.

  7. Fitzmyer, COS 2.82 (p. 215). Likewise, the Hittite treaty mentioned earlier threatens Huqqana if he should violate its terms by seeking another ally:

    No. 3 §9 (A ii 2–9) If you act thus, these oath deities will not leave you alone, nor on your account will they leave alone that man to whom you go over. They shall destroy him... They shall destroy both of you together and thereby fulfill the wishes of My Majesty (Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts, 29).

    These same gods are the agents of promised good for keeping the treaty’s terms (§9 [A ii 10–13]).

  8. Translation follows Ibn Ezra’s Commentary on the Pentateuch, trans. and annot. by H. Norman Strickman and Arthur M. Silver (New York: Menorah Pub., 1988–2004). The same sentiment is present in Ibn Ezra’s comments on Deuteronomy 30:19.

  9. The Assyrian texts are available online through the State Archive of Assyria project. For a description and introduction, see Jonathan Taylor, “The Succession Treaties of Esarhaddon,” Nimrud: Materialities of Assyrian Knowledge Production, The Nimrud Project at Oracc.org, 2019. The name “Esarhaddon’s Succession Treaty” is assigned to the text in the edition by Simo Parpola and Kazuko Watanabe, Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths, State Archives of Assyria 2 (Helsinki: Helsinki University Press, 1988), 28–58 (No. 6). This designation best reflects the text’s purpose. The first edition of the text used the name “The Vassal-Treaties of Esarhaddon,” because all the copies name foreign, conquered vassal governors as parties to the treaties. See D. J. Wiseman, “The Vassal-Treaties of Esarhaddon,” Iraq 20 (1958): 27. However, the language of the treaties makes it clear that the entire Assyrian population, and not just the vassals, were subject to similar terms. See Parpola and Watanabe, “The Treaty Corpus.” For discussion of the particular relevance of these treaties to the Book of Deuteronomy and its date, see Bernard M. Levinson and Jeffrey Stackert, “Between the Covenant Code and Esarhaddon’s Succession Treaty: Deuteronomy 13 and the Composition of Deuteronomy,” Journal of Ancient Judaism 3 (2012): 123–140.

  10. The gods of heaven and earth appear again, twice, in the treaty’s curse sections (ll. 472, 523). Translation follows Parpola and Watanabe, Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths, 28–58 (No. 6).

  11. Descriptions of the seals, the legends, and the dating, here and in the discussion below, follow Parpola and Watanabe, “Structural and Formal Analysis,” Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths, xxxvi, with modifications.

  12. This is especially important because the treaty’s main purpose is to protect the line of succession in favor of Assurbanipal, Esarhaddon’s son. After all, the treaty only really takes effect following the death of its promulgator.

  13. Mullissu was the divine consort of Assur, the head of the Assyrian pantheon. She is identified with Ninlil, the wife of Enlil, who was head of the Mesopotamian pantheon. See Nicole Brisch, “Ninlil (Mulliltu, Mullissu, Mylitta) (goddess),” Ancient Mesopotamian Gods and Goddesses, ORACC and the UK Higher Education Academy, 2019.

  14. Parpola and Watanabe, Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths, 45.

  15. Ibn Ezra rejects the idea that calling heaven and earth as witnesses is a direct reference to rain:

    אבן עזרא דברים ד:כו ואחרים אמרו על הגשם כטעם את שמיכם כברזל ואת ארצכם כנחושה [ויקרא כו:יט].
    Ibn Ezra Deut 4:26 Others say that the reference is to the rain, as in “and I will make your heaven as iron, and your earth as brass” (Lev 26:19).
